subject: Psychiatry
summary: Antipsychotics treat psychotic disorders by modulating dopamine and other neurotransmitters. In low‑resource hospitals, clinicians must prioritize clinical diagnosis, use limited investigations wisely, and monitor for serious adverse effects such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

sections.p: Psychotic disorders are characterised by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought or behaviour, and negative symptoms. Diagnosis relies on DSM‑5 or ICD‑10 criteria, but in low‑resource settings a focused mental status exam and collateral history are essential.
b: Positive symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder
Negative symptoms: affective flattening, avolition, alogia
Duration >1 month for schizophrenia; shorter for brief psychotic disorder

sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and level of monitoring. Use the Clinical Global Impression‑Severity (CGI‑S) scale (1 = normal, 7 = most severely ill).
b: Mild (CGI‑S 1‑3): outpatient, low‑dose oral antipsychotic
Moderate (CGI‑S 4‑5): inpatient observation, consider depot formulation
Severe (CGI‑S 6‑7): urgent admission, monitor for NMS, consider rapid‑acting IM haloperidol

sections.p: Psychosis may be primary (schizophrenia, bipolar mania) or secondary to medical illness, substance use, or medication.
b: Primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia, schizoaffective)
Secondary to HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder
Malaria cerebral or severe malaria with delirium
Tuberculosis meningitis
Substance‑induced (cannabis, amphetamines, alcohol withdrawal)
Medication‑induced (corticosteroids, anti‑malarial drugs)
Electrolyte disturbance (hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia)

sections.p: Patients may be brought by family with agitation, bizarre behaviour, or inability to care for themselves. Look for a pattern of symptoms, recent stressors, and physical signs of infection or substance use.
b: Acute agitation with verbal or physical aggression
Fixed false beliefs (e.g., witchcraft accusations)
Auditory hallucinations commenting on actions
Neglect of personal hygiene, weight loss
Signs of infection: fever, neck stiffness (TB meningitis)

sections.p: Prioritise tests that change management; when unavailable, rely on clinical clues.

t.b: Detect infection, anemia, or leukopenia from antipsychotics; normal result does not exclude infection
Identify HIV‑related psychosis; if unavailable, use risk assessment and treat empirically if high suspicion
Rule out metabolic causes (e.g., hyponatraemia); treat abnormal values before antipsychotic initiation
Identify stimulant or cannabis intoxication; if unavailable, obtain detailed substance use history
Exclude structural lesions; if not available, assess for focal neurological signs

sections.p: Early recognition of life‑threatening adverse effects saves lives.
b: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: fever > 38 °C, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status
Severe extrapyramidal symptoms (tardive dyskinesia, acute dystonia)
Suicidal ideation or self‑harm
Uncontrolled hypertension or tachycardia from certain atypicals

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, start an antipsychotic, and monitor for side effects. Choose agents based on efficacy, side‑effect profile, and availability.
b: First‑generation: haloperidol IM/PO – rapid control, high EPS risk; avoid in Parkinson’s disease
Second‑generation: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole – lower EPS, monitor weight, glucose, lipids
Adjunctive benzodiazepine (lorazepam) for severe agitation or NMS suspicion
Avoid high‑potency FGAs in patients with cardiac disease or severe dehydration

sections.p: Regular review of symptom control, side‑effects, and adherence is essential. In low‑resource settings, use community health workers for medication delivery and psycho‑education.
b: Re‑assess CGI‑S every 2 weeks until stable
Monitor weight, blood pressure, fasting glucose every 3 months for SGAs
Screen for EPS at each visit; treat with benztropine if needed
Educate family about early signs of relapse and NMS

sections.p: Conditions that mimic psychosis can lead to misdiagnosis.
b: Delirium from infection or metabolic disturbance – fluctuating consciousness, attention deficit
Acute mania – elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep
Severe depression with psychotic features – pervasive low mood, guilt, suicidal thoughts

sections.p: Lab and clinical findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CBC does not rule out early TB meningitis
Negative urine drug screen may miss recent cannabis use (short detection window)
Absence of fever does not exclude NMS early in its course

whenToSeekHelp: Fever > 38 °C with rigidity and autonomic instability (possible NMS)
Sudden loss of consciousness or seizures

faq.q: Why choose risperidone over haloperidol in a young adult?
faq.a: Risperidone has lower risk of acute dystonia and tardive dyskinesia, which are especially problematic for long‑term adherence.

faq.q: Can antipsychotics be used in patients with HIV?
faq.a: Yes, but monitor for drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals and for metabolic side‑effects.

faq.q: What is the first step if neuroleptic malignant syndrome is suspected?
faq.a: Stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care, and start a benzodiazepine; consider dantrolene if available.

exam: A 22‑year‑old with new‑onset auditory hallucinations and weight loss is brought from a rural clinic. Which investigations are essential before starting antipsychotics? — HIV test, electrolytes, CBC, and screen for substance use; imaging only if focal signs.

During admission, the patient develops fever = 38.5 °C, muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. What is your immediate management? — Stop antipsychotic, initiate supportive care, give IV benzodiazepine, monitor vitals; consider dantrolene if available.

You must choose an antipsychotic for a patient with a history of epilepsy. Which drug is least appropriate and why? — Haloperidol is less suitable because high‑potency FGAs can lower seizure threshold; a SGA such as olanzapine is preferred.

A patient on risperidone reports involuntary tongue movements after 6 months. What is the likely diagnosis and next step? — Tardive dyskinesia; consider switching to a different class and add benztropine if symptoms are severe.

In a low‑resource hospital without serum lipid testing, how do you monitor metabolic side‑effects of SGAs? — Track weight, waist circumference, and blood pressure; educate patient on diet and exercise; refer for labs when possible.

Explain the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia and how antipsychotics address it. — Excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway produces positive symptoms; antipsychotics block D2 receptors, reducing this activity.

A patient on olanzapine develops new‑onset polyuria and polydipsia. What should you suspect and how to confirm? — Possible diabetes mellitus; obtain fasting glucose or HbA1c; adjust medication if hyperglycaemia confirmed.
